title: Functional significance and the gene dose effect

segs.text: Section two. Functional significance and the gene dose effect. An allele name is useful only once its functional significance is known: what the variant does to the activity of the protein the gene codes for, an enzyme, transporter or receptor. It is about activity, not how common the variant is. Labs made these variant enzymes and measured their activity against the wild type, so genotype, the alleles, and phenotype, the activity, are tightly linked.

The same star number means different things in different genes. Star one is normal activity in both sip two C nineteen and sip two C nine. In two C nineteen, star two and star three have no activity; both make a short, truncated protein that does not function. In two C nine, star two and star three have decreased activity. So star two does not mean no activity in every gene.

Each person has two alleles of each gene, one from each parent; the pair is the genotype, written two C nineteen star one, star two. Two different alleles make you heterozygous, two the same homozygous. The two copies' activity adds up: star one, star one is normal; star one with star two or star three is about halfway, because one copy makes active enzyme and the other none. She called this the gene dose effect. There is no dominance in these drug-response variants.

Any pair of inactive alleles, star two, star two, star two, star three, or star three, star three, has no activity. Heterozygous does not by itself mean partial activity; star two, star three has none. Induction, raising the amount of enzyme with diet or other drugs, cannot rescue star two, because the protein is too short to function.
